note: HAND-MAINTAINED — the sweep never writes this file. Every survivor mutation-sweep-state.json records must be given a verdict here before its target counts as SWEPT_CLEAN. A survivor is an accepted equivalent, a missing pin, or dead code; only a human can say which, and a tool that triaged its own survivors would be a record agreeing with itself.

verdicts.equivalent: the mutant changes no observable behaviour — accept it, and NAME the class below. Never silently re-tally it.
verdicts.pinned: it was a real gap; a test now kills it. The entry records where that test lives, so the claim is checkable.
verdicts.dead-code: the mutated code is genuinely unreachable and was deleted. If the entry still exists, the deletion has not happened.

classes.degenerate-zero: a guard where `x <= 0` -> `x < 0` (or the mirror) yields the same output because zero already produces zero: feeCentsOfTotal(0), rebalanceEthNeedRaw(0n), a zero weight mapping to zero. A family law in batcher.test.ts asserts the property once over every helper and every degenerate shape rather than pinning them one by one.
classes.layered-guard: deleting an outer condition leaves an INNER check that refuses identically, so the mutant is unobservable at the module boundary. UIGuy measured this on assemble-batch (2026-08-07): six tests against the highest-value survivors killed exactly ONE. The cheap way to tell before writing anything is to force the outer condition and see whether an inner layer still refuses. Named, not chased.
classes.unobservable-then-refused: the mutant DOES create a bad record, but the only path that reaches it guarantees the record is discarded before it can be read — the chain is refused and deleted, or the assembler's own filter drops the artefact. Distinct from layered-guard: nothing refuses the mutant, the evidence is simply thrown away. Fragile by nature, so each entry must name the discard step, because adding any consumer AFTER that step re-opens it.
classes.defensive-redundancy: the guard never fires today because an upstream invariant makes its condition always true, so widening it selects the same set. It is a belt to someone else's braces and its equivalence DEPENDS on that invariant — the entry must name the invariant, since the mutant stops being equivalent the moment the invariant breaks, which is precisely when the guard earns its place.
classes.unreachable-by-fixture: NOT a verdict — this is the desk-236-M10/M11 question itself. A survivor in a path the module's fixtures never construct is either dead code or an untested path, and those want opposite fixes. It stays UNTRIAGED until a fixture reaches it (then it becomes pinned or equivalent) or it is proven unreachable (then dead-code).
